contribution: The course's world map: students use the Global Fusion Explorer (60 facilities, year, status, country and type filters) to compare the Cold-War geography of fusion research with today's networks, read the data critically (selection, unknown years, today's country names) and connect the map with the course timeline.
learn: compare the geography of fusion research during the Cold War with today's network, using a data map.
explain how declassification, verification and cost turned competition into collaboration.
evaluate the limits of a facility map: selection, unknown years and company-reported results.
prior: The T-3 results of 1968 were confirmed by a British team in 1969 (chapter *Science across the Iron Curtain*)
ITER began with the 1985 Geneva summit and has seven members (chapter *ITER: why, where and who*)

activities.text: In 1955 a fusion physicist in Princeton could not tell a colleague in Moscow what she was working on: both worked in secret, on opposite sides of the Iron Curtain. Today, physicists from China, India, Russia, the United States and Europe build one machine together in southern France and share their data by e-mail every day. Somewhere between these two pictures, the map of fusion research changed.
activities.question: How did fusion research move from secret national projects to a worldwide network, and how can a map show it?

activities.title: Review: science across the Iron Curtain
activities.prompt: In the chapter *Science across the Iron Curtain*, you met the T-3 tokamak. Why was the British measurement of T-3 in 1969 so important?

choices.text: It checked a surprising Soviet result independently, so others believed it.
choices.feedback: Right. A British team measured the plasma with their own laser and confirmed about ten million degrees. After this independent check, laboratories around the world started building tokamaks.

choices.text: It was the first time that a tokamak produced electricity.
choices.feedback: No tokamak has ever produced electricity. The 1969 measurement checked the temperature of T-3's plasma.

choices.text: It showed that the Soviet results had been invented for propaganda.
choices.feedback: The opposite: the British measurement confirmed the Soviet result, about ten million degrees.

choices.text: It started the secret period of fusion research in Britain.
choices.feedback: Fusion research had been declassified in 1958. The 1969 visit was possible because the field had become open.

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • During the Cold War, fusion research was probably …
  • Today I think research is done in …, because …
  • A map could show … but not …

activities.title: Think about it: a map of science
activities.pair: Pair work: share your ideas aloud, then each of you writes.
activities.prompt: Discuss with a partner, then write two or three sentences. Where do you think fusion research was done in the 1950s, and where is it done today? What can a map of fusion facilities show about history, and what can it not show?
activities.model: During the Cold War, fusion research was probably done in a few rich countries with nuclear weapons, such as the United States and the Soviet Union. Today I think research is done in many countries, including China, Japan and Europe, because the machines are very expensive and countries cooperate. A map could show where and when machines were built, but not what the scientists said to each other or how good their results were.
criteria: The answer suggests a difference between the 1950s and today.
The answer gives a reason for the change (for example politics, cost, cooperation).
The answer names one thing a map can show and one thing it cannot.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the early map
activities.prompt: The explorer lists 60 facilities. In how many countries does it show fusion machines that **started before 1970**?

choices.text: In 3 countries
choices.feedback: Right: the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, the three nuclear powers that ran secret fusion programmes and declassified them together in 1958. Remember that the explorer is a selection: smaller programmes elsewhere are missing.

choices.text: In 7 countries
choices.feedback: The explorer shows early machines in only three: the United States (Model A to C, Perhapsatron, Scylla), the United Kingdom (ZETA) and the Soviet Union (T-1, T-3). Fusion research began in secret in the nuclear powers.

choices.text: In 12 countries
choices.feedback: Twelve is the number of countries with *operating* facilities in 2026. Before 1970 the explorer shows machines in only three: the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union.

choices.text: In 20 countries
choices.feedback: The whole explorer, all years together, has facilities in only 14 countries. Before 1970 it shows three: the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the map today
activities.prompt: In how many countries does the explorer show facilities that are **operating** in 2026, and on how many continents?

choices.text: 4 countries on 2 continents
choices.feedback: The network is much wider: 12 countries on three continents (Europe, North America and Asia). China, Japan, South Korea and India all operate machines.

choices.text: 12 countries on 3 continents
choices.feedback: Right: the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Switzerland, Spain, Russia, China, Japan, South Korea and India. Many of their machines prepare ITER or test its parts.

choices.text: 25 countries on 5 continents
choices.feedback: Too many for this selection: 12 countries on three continents (Europe, North America and Asia). The whole explorer, all years together, covers only 14 countries.

choices.text: 6 countries, all of them in Europe
choices.feedback: Europe has many machines, but so do North America and Asia: 12 countries on three continents in 2026.

activities.title: The Global Fusion Explorer
activities.text: The map loads its background from OpenStreetMap, so it needs an internet connection. The list and the panels work even without the map.

activities.title: Missions: from competition to collaboration
activities.text:
Work in pairs and write your findings in a table with the columns *year*, *facilities*, *countries* and *notes*.

1. **The secret years.** Untick *any year* and move the year slider to **1958**. Which facilities and countries does the list show? Open ZETA and T-1. (Ignore lines that end in *–?* after their real working life: the end year is unknown.)
2. **Before 1970.** Tick *any year* again and look at the start years in the list: which countries had machines that started before 1970? Search for **T-3**: why does it never appear under a year?
3. **The age of big machines.** Set the year to **1985**. Count the facilities and countries again, leaving out the old machines with unknown end years (such as Model A, 1953–?). Which machine is shared by several countries? Open its panel.
4. **Today's network.** Tick *any year*, choose the status **Operating** and count the countries in the list. Then choose *Under construction* and *Planned*: who builds new machines?
5. **Machines that cross borders.** Open the panels of ITER, JT-60SA, HL-2A and COMPASS. Note for each one which countries are involved.
6. **Back to the timeline.** Open the unit [Fusion history: an interactive timeline](fy14-fusion-timeline.html), find the events of 1958, 1969 and 1985, and follow a *Show on the map* link back to this explorer.

Word bank

site · facility · device · operating · retired · under construction · planned · to cluster · to spread · to share · a joint project · a network · secrecy · the Cold War

Sentence starters

  • In 1958 the list shows … facilities in … countries.
  • By 1985, … had joined, and … was shared by …
  • In 2026, operating facilities stand in …
  • The biggest change is that …
  • One limitation of the data is …

activities.title: Record and compare your findings
activities.pair: Pair work: one of you operates the explorer, the other writes; swap roles after mission 3.
activities.prompt: Discuss with your partner, then write four or five sentences from your table. How many facilities and countries did you find in 1958, in 1985 and in 2026 (operating)? Which machines involve several countries? Name one limitation of the data that affected your counts.
activities.model: In 1958 the list shows six facilities in three countries: the United States (Model A, Model B, the Perhapsatron and Scylla I), the United Kingdom (ZETA) and the Soviet Union (T-1). By 1985, leaving out old machines with unknown end years, it shows seven machines in five countries: the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, Japan and West Germany, and JET in the UK was shared by European countries. In 2026, operating facilities stand in 12 countries on three continents, from Canada to South Korea. ITER (seven members), JT-60SA (Japan and Europe), HL-2A (built from German ASDEX parts in China) and COMPASS (from the UK to the Czech Republic) cross borders. One limitation of the data is that machines with unknown years, such as T-3, are counted wrongly or not at all by the year filter.
criteria: The answer gives counts of facilities or countries for at least two different years.
The answer names at least two machines that involve several countries and says which countries.
The answer describes the change from a few countries to many.
The answer names a limitation of the data (selection, unknown years, today's country names, company-reported results).

Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with your own counts and with the story. In one or two sentences: what changed the geography of fusion research most?

activities.title: Write a museum label
activities.prompt: Imagine the explorer becomes an exhibition. Choose one facility (not ITER) and write its museum label of 60–90 words. Use the facts in its panel: name, place, type, years, one achievement with its date, and why it matters for the story *from competition to collaboration*. Write in your own words.
activities.model: **JET, Culham, United Kingdom (1983–2023).** The Joint European Torus was a tokamak built and run by European countries together, under a joint undertaking set up in 1978. For 40 years it was the largest tokamak in the world. In 1997 it produced $16\ \text{MW}$ of fusion power, and in 2023 it released $69\ \text{MJ}$ of fusion energy in a single pulse. JET matters because it showed that only countries working together can afford the biggest fusion machines: it was the model for ITER.
criteria: The label gives name, place, type and years from the panel.
The label gives one achievement with its date and keeps results and plans apart.
The label explains why the facility matters for competition or collaboration.
The label is 60–90 words and written in the writer's own words.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student sets the year slider to 1965 and writes: *"In 1965 nobody in the Soviet Union did fusion research: the list shows only American and British machines."* What is wrong with this conclusion?

choices.text: The data is a selection, and T-3, whose start year is unknown, is hidden.
choices.feedback: Right. T-3 was running in Moscow in the 1960s, but the explorer has no exact start year for it, so the year filter never shows it. An empty country in a selection is a gap in the data, not proof of no research.

choices.text: Nothing: the Soviet Union stopped its fusion research from 1959 to 1975.
choices.feedback: The Soviet Union never stopped: T-3 produced the famous results of 1968. The year filter hides T-3 because its start year is unknown.

choices.text: The slider shows only machines built in exactly 1965.
choices.feedback: The slider shows machines *operating* in that year, not only those built then. The problem is the missing start year of T-3 and the selection of the data.

choices.text: Soviet machines appear under Russia, so the student chose the wrong country.
choices.feedback: The country filter uses today's names, but the student used the year slider, not the country filter. T-3 is hidden because its start year is unknown.

activities.title: 1. History: the turning point
activities.prompt: Which event made fusion research open to scientists of all countries?

choices.text: The UN atomic energy conference in Geneva in 1958
choices.feedback: Right. The United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom declassified their fusion research there and presented it in detail.

choices.text: The Reagan–Gorbachev summit in Geneva in 1985
choices.feedback: The 1985 summit started the idea of ITER, but fusion research had already been open since the 1958 conference in the same city.

choices.text: The signing of the ITER Agreement in Paris in 2006
choices.feedback: By 2006 fusion research had been open for almost fifty years. It became open at the 1958 Geneva conference.

choices.text: The first plasma of the T-1 tokamak in Moscow in 1958
choices.feedback: T-1 was a Soviet machine, not an act of openness. The declassification came at the Geneva conference of September 1958.

activities.title: 2. Data: reading the explorer
activities.prompt: The list shows *NSTX, 1999–?*. What does the question mark mean, and what does it do to the year filter?

choices.text: No end year is known, so the filter shows NSTX in every later year.
choices.feedback: Right. The data has no end year for NSTX, so the filter keeps it in every later year, although it was rebuilt as NSTX-U. Check such lines yourself.

choices.text: NSTX is still operating, so the filter shows it correctly.
choices.feedback: An operating machine has *today* as its end. *–?* means that the end year is unknown; NSTX was in fact rebuilt as NSTX-U.

choices.text: The start year is uncertain, so the filter hides NSTX.
choices.feedback: The start year, 1999, is known. The question mark replaces the *end* year, and then the filter keeps showing the machine.

choices.text: NSTX is planned, so the filter shows it only after 1999.
choices.feedback: NSTX is retired, not planned. *–?* means only that its end year is unknown.

activities.title: 3. Collaboration: which machine?
activities.prompt: Which facility in the explorer is the best example of international collaboration in the building of one machine?

choices.text: JT-60SA, built by Japan and Europe together
choices.feedback: Right. JT-60SA at Naka was built and is run by Japan and the European Union. ITER, JET and HL-2A are other examples.

choices.text: ZETA, Britain's large pinch machine of 1957
choices.feedback: ZETA was a national, at first secret, British project. It shows the competition of the 1950s, not collaboration.

choices.text: T-1, the first Soviet tokamak of 1958
choices.feedback: T-1 was a national Soviet machine. Collaboration came later, for example with the British measurement of T-3 in 1969.

choices.text: Perhapsatron, a secret Los Alamos pinch
choices.feedback: The Perhapsatron was part of a secret US programme in the 1950s, an example of competition, not collaboration.

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • During the Cold War, fusion machines stood only in …
  • Today, the map shows …
  • The change happened because …
  • However, the data has limits: …
  • Competition has not disappeared: …

activities.title: 4. Write: from competition to collaboration
activities.prompt: Write a paragraph of 100–140 words. Compare the geography of fusion research during the Cold War with today's network. Use at least two pieces of evidence from the explorer (counts, facilities or panels) and one event from the timeline, explain why the change happened, and name one limit of the data.
activities.model: During the Cold War, fusion machines in the explorer stood only in the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, and until 1958 their research was secret. Today, operating facilities stand in 12 countries on three continents, and the largest machine, ITER, is built by seven members. The change happened because the 1958 Geneva conference made the field open, because surprising results such as T-3's needed independent checks, and because machines became too expensive for one country: JET (1978) and ITER (agreement in 2006) were shared. Machines even crossed borders, like Germany's ASDEX, which became HL-2A in China. However, the data has limits: it is a selection, and machines with unknown years, such as T-3, are missing from the year filter. Competition has not disappeared: countries and companies still race for records.
criteria: The answer describes the Cold War geography (few countries, secrecy) and today's network with evidence from the explorer.
The answer uses at least one dated event (1958, 1969, 1978, 1985 or 2006).
The answer explains at least one reason for the change.
The answer names a limitation of the data.
The answer is 100–140 words with clear linking words (*because*, *however*).

activities.text:
Le coin français

The biggest marker on the map is in France. Listen, repeat, and show your partner ITER on the map while you say the last sentence. In the hints, capitals show the stressed syllable, and õ, ã, ẽ are nasal vowels: the air goes through the nose and no n is heard.
